retrieval_text: The patient is a 37-year-old male from a non-consanguineous Chinese family. At age 35, he began to experience progressive weakness in his hands, with a notable reduction in grip strength, particularly in the right hand. Six months later, muscle atrophy and fibrillation were observed in his hands, leading to an inability to hold objects or write. One year later, he developed weakness in his lower extremities without sensory disturbances. He currently has difficulty climbing stairs, standing up from a squatting position, lifting his foot upward, and frequently trips. Physical examination showed normal cranial nerves and no orolingual fasciculations or atrophy. Neck flexion strength was rated 5 on the MRC muscle scale (grades 0–5). Muscle strength on both sides was as follows: triceps and biceps 3/3, forearm flexors 2/2, intrinsic hand muscles 1/1, iliopsoas muscles 4/4, quadriceps muscles 3/3, tibialis anterior and gastrocnemius muscles 2/2. Deep tendon reflexes were absent. There were no sensory abnormalities or coordination difficulties in any limbs. Muscle atrophy was prominent, especially in the interosseous muscles of the hands, bilateral gastrocnemius, and anterior tibial muscles. Muscle fibrillation was noted in the biceps and quadriceps muscles. Serum creatine kinase level was 668 U/L (normal range: 50–310 U/L).

The patient is a 6-month-old male child born to a non-consanguineous, phenotypically normal couple. He was delivered at 39 weeks of gestation via cesarean section with a birth weight of 2,820 grams. At 6 months, his weight was 5.6 kg (<3rd percentile), his height was 63 cm (<3rd percentile), and his head circumference was 46 cm (90th percentile). The patient exhibited poor growth and developmental delays, including the absence of social smiling and maternal recognition by 12 months of age. Mild dysmorphic features were noted.

A 24-year-old male visited the dermatology outpatient department with lifelong thickening of the skin on his palms and soles, which had progressively spread to the backs of his hands and feet over the past 5 years. He reported recurrent blistering and painful cracks on his palms. For the past 6 months, he had hyperpigmented, raised, scaly plaques on the extensor surfaces of both knees and elbows. Additionally, he experienced redness and mildly painful fissures at the corners of his mouth for the same duration. He had no other systemic issues and no family history of similar symptoms. On physical examination, there was widespread thickening of the skin on the palms and soles, extending to the backs of the hands and feet, with irregular, poorly defined borders and prominent knuckle pads. The skin on the palms and soles appeared thick, waxy, yellowish, and emitted an unpleasant odor, with a loss of normal skin patterns. There were multiple erosions and fissures of varying sizes on both palms, and pitted keratolysis on the soles. The fingers exhibited a pseudosclerodermatous appearance, with some showing conical tapering and digital constrictions at various points, along with mild flexion deformity. The nails were thickened and hypercurved, with dystrophic changes noted in both great toenails. The patient also had multiple hyperkeratotic, scaly, irregular, and poorly defined plaques on the extensor surfaces of both elbows and knees. Additionally, the lower lip was dry, erythematous, and thickened, with angular cheilitis.

A 26-year-old otherwise healthy, nulligravida female presented to the emergency department with worsening right lower quadrant pain, diarrhea, nausea, and vomiting for four days. She also reported low back discomfort and abdominal discomfort, which she attributed to forceful vomiting. She had taken a muscle relaxant earlier that morning, but the pain in her right lower quadrant persisted. Her primary care physician advised her to go to the emergency department for evaluation. Over the past two years, she had experienced recurrent and increasing abdominal discomfort, increased heartburn, right and left lower quadrant pain with back pain, and fluctuating periods of diarrhea and constipation. She had been seen in the same emergency department 12 months prior and was treated for a urinary tract infection with antibiotics.

A 49-year-old male reported visual impairment in his left eye for over 20 years, which he had previously ignored. He visited the hospital on March 3, 2020, with a primary complaint of visual disturbance in his right eye that began the previous year. Family history revealed no notable abnormalities.

A 39-year-old woman reported experiencing decreased vision in her right eye (OD) for the past year, accompanied by watering and redness in the same eye. She observed an irregular increase in the size of her pupil in OD. There was no history of trauma or previous surgeries. She had been prescribed brimonidine and timolol maleate combination therapy for glaucoma in OD. Upon examination, her visual acuity in OD was 6/12, improving to 6/6 with pinhole, and in her left eye (OS) was 6/6.

A 38-year-old male patient presented with a long-standing history of multiple non-tender scalp swellings ranging from 2.5 to 3.5 cm in diameter, which have progressively grown over the past year. The skin over the swellings appeared normal. Clinical examination showed multiple nodular lesions coalesced on the anterior region of the scalp, which were solid and movable from the underlying surface.

A 16-year-old female presented with thickened skin on the palms and soles, cracked lips, mild scaling on the buttocks, and fissures on the fingers and feet. Additionally, there were erosions on the perianal, vaginal, and nasal mucosa, along with widespread hair loss and sparse hair growth. Nail abnormalities and a hyperkeratotic plaque around the perianal area were also observed. The patient has congenital deafness, delayed speech, and developmental and learning challenges.

A 54-year-old male was referred to the Rheumatology Division of Fornaroli Hospital from the Infective Department. In February 2014, he was admitted to the hospital due to interstitial lung disease of uncertain origin, presenting with fever accompanied by shivering, dry cough, and chest pain.

A 50-year-old man, with no prior medical history, was admitted to the hospital presenting with shortness of breath and upper abdominal pain. His heart rate was recorded at 130 beats per minute and blood pressure at 110/60 mmHg. Physical examination revealed significantly distended jugular veins and a gallop rhythm.
A 34-year-old female presented with a primary complaint of rapid vision loss in the right eye over three months.

A 10-year-old girl was seen by a neurologist at the OPD Neurology, Pakistan Institute of Medical Sciences hospital, Islamabad, for evaluation of congenital microcephaly and seizures. Her family history revealed that her 8-year-old sister exhibited similar characteristics. The patient presented with short stature, a slim body, and distinct facial features including a narrow forehead, bulging eyes, a pointed nose, fuller lips, a broad mouth, and constant drooling. An ophthalmic examination indicated reduced vision due to retinal lesions and bilateral cataracts. She demonstrated good control of her head and other body parts, recognized her parents socially, and was observed smiling. Both children experienced developmental delays, learning disabilities, repetitive behavior, absence of speech, and mood disturbances. The mother reported no viral infections or medication use during the full-term pregnancy, and the delivery was normal.

A 7-year-old boy from southwest China presented with blue cornea, photophobia, and poor vision since birth. At 36 days old, he underwent bilateral anti-glaucoma surgery, followed by long-term use of travoprost and brinzolamide eye drops. Despite this, intraocular pressure remained poorly controlled. The patient also had surgeries for an atrial septal defect and a sublingual cyst. Recently, his eye symptoms worsened, and his vision deteriorated significantly. Consequently, the boy and his family sought medical attention at the Affiliated Hospital of Southwest Medical University. A three-generational family pedigree is available.

A 47-year-old male presented with abdominal pain persisting for 3 days. He had a history of acute appendicitis 10 years ago, for which he underwent an appendectomy. He had no history of hypertension or diabetes mellitus. The patient was an ex-smoker and a social drinker. It was noted that he consumed raw anchovies 4 days prior to the onset of symptoms. Upon admission, his vital signs were as follows: blood pressure 120/70 mm Hg, pulse rate 68/min, respiration rate 16/min, and body temperature 37℃. There were no signs of urticaria or facial angioedema. Abdominal examination revealed no splenomegaly or palpable mass, but there was epigastric and periumbilical tenderness without rebound tenderness. Digital rectal examination was unremarkable.

An 18-year-old female presented with a primary concern of forwardly positioned teeth in the upper front region of the jaw. Family history indicated similar features in her father and grandmother. Extraoral examination showed an upward slant of the eye openings with sparse eyelashes on the lower eyelids. There was underdevelopment of the cheekbones and a small lower jaw. The upper jaw appeared to be protruding, giving the face a distinctive appearance. Intraoral examination found a narrow, high-arched palate. The upper front teeth were angled forward with spacing between the upper and lower front teeth. Root remnants were observed in the positions of teeth 26, 36, and 46. There was generalized gum recession and grade I tooth mobility.

A 17-year-old girl, born in Italy, with parents who are not related and do not have similar conditions. She is the younger sibling of another case. At birth, she presented with cleft lip and palate, facial abnormalities, foot deformities, and was described as a collodion baby. The initial examination was conducted when she was 3 years old, during which her parents reported allergic reactions affecting her eyes and sensitivity to light. Upon inspection, the palisades of Vogt and meibomian glands were absent. Conjunctival swelling, tear film instability, and a reduced tear meniscus were noted. Annual monitoring of her ocular condition showed stability up to the last visit in March 2023. At that time, mucus secretions in the eyes were observed, and some eyelashes in abnormal positions were removed. The patient uses daily ocular lubricants, anti-inflammatory eyedrops, and lipid-based tear film stabilizers.

A 7-year and 5-month-old Chinese boy, the second child of healthy, non-consanguineous parents, presented with delayed motor development from birth. He achieved head and neck stability at 7 months, rolled over at 11 months, and walked independently at 2 years. His language development was significantly delayed. At 2 years old, he experienced his first epileptic episode, characterized by eye staring, lip cyanosis, foaming at the mouth, and limb jerks, lasting for several minutes.

A 19-month-old girl presented with haemolytic anaemia and developmental delay. She was the first child of third-cousin parents, born at 38 weeks following an uncomplicated pregnancy. She was hospitalized in the neonatal intensive care unit for 38 days due to neonatal jaundice and early sepsis, requiring five blood transfusions immediately after birth and an exchange transfusion on the second day of life due to maternal-foetal ABO incompatibility. Another blood transfusion was required at 30 days old for non-spherocytic haemolytic anaemia. At 9 months, she experienced multiple haemolytic crises triggered by infections and exhibited mild psychomotor developmental delay, unable to sit independently.

A 10-month-old male of Indian descent with a history of atopic dermatitis and egg allergy presented to the outpatient clinic with rhinorrhea and decreased oral intake. His birth history was unremarkable, and immunizations were current. He was initially treated for an upper respiratory infection. Two days later, he returned with additional symptoms including diffuse facial swelling and redness, perioral skin irritation, and right-sided ear pain. Augmentin was prescribed for right-sided otitis media, and topical mupirocin was applied to crusted skin on the right side of his face and upper right perioral region. Rapid COVID-19 and Influenza A and B tests were negative. Due to concerns about a possible allergic reaction, parents were advised to administer an antihistamine and monitor the facial swelling, with instructions to return if symptoms did not improve. That evening, the patient developed a fever of 100.4 °F and was taken to the emergency department at a local children's hospital. The parents were advised to continue the current treatment regimen. Over the next 48 hours, the patient's facial swelling worsened, and he developed swelling in both extremities and widespread skin peeling. Upon returning to the emergency department, initial vital signs showed a heart rate of 137 and a blood pressure of 136/108.

An 8-month-old boy, born to consanguineous parents, presented with persistent seizures and significant developmental delays. Physical examination revealed a small head size with overlapping sutures, a small jaw, a large right ear, and a narrow forehead. Eye examination showed dislocated lenses.
